title: The Crack in the Ledger
sceneText:
Sorting through the papers Hartmann left, you find that the last two months do not come out.

It is not a large sum. It is a series of small payments, three to five guldmark each, at irregular intervals, the summary column giving “sundry expenditure” for every one. Together they come to under twenty guldmark, which in a month of an estate’s turnover is next to invisible.

You copy them onto a sheet by date and look at it for a long time.

What stops you is not the amount. It is that the date, the sum and the person handling it are recorded exactly for every one of them, in the same hand as every other page. Neat, unshaken, nothing corrected.

A man who wanted to cover something would not record it that clearly.

He was keeping a record, not concealing one. He was leaving somebody a copy.

On the expenditure budget at the back you look twice, and you are not on it.

Your pay is not in this ledger. It comes out of the Baron’s private budget in Forgehold, in a different system from the stable repairs, the tenants’ seed money, the kitchen buying. You account for every guldmark on this estate, and you yourself are one line in another book.

That book you cannot see.

choices.text: Go on with it, and find out who the money went to

effects.logEntry: You began looking properly into the irregular entries in the ledger.

choices.resultText:
You sat with it another afternoon.

There is no payee named against those payments, only a reference: three letters and two digits, the same on all eight. You look for the reference on other pages, and you find it. It appears in the payment column of a carriage contract from three years ago.

The contract is Millridge’s.

You turned the corner of the page down.

Then you sat a while, and smoothed the corner flat again. You do not know who you were arguing with.

effects.logEntry: You wrote to Baron von Alder reporting the irregularity in the accounts.

choices.resultText:
The letter came out short. You wrote it three times and each version was shorter.

What finally went out was four lines: the state of the accounts as you took them over, the inconsistency you had found, what you intended to do about it, and a line asking him to be aware of it.

When Elena came to collect what was going out, she glanced at the address on the envelope.

She said nothing.

Three days later Martha asked you in the kitchen whether there had been any reply from Forgehold.

You had not told anybody that you wrote.

choices.text: Leave it. The harvest matters more

effects.logEntry: You set the ledger question aside and put the harvest first.

choices.resultText:
You close those pages and put them back where they were.

The wheat is in the fields. That is the one thing that cannot wait.

You push the ledger to the corner of the desk, underneath a stack of tenant rolls. The next day you find it in the same place, except that Elena, tidying, has drawn it out and set it on top.

She probably thought you were looking for it.
